Strategic Report

The directors present their strategic report for the year ended 31 March 2024.

Business Review
The company continues to operate as a wholesale supplier and distributor of artisan bakery goods, ambient pantry lines, and specialist flours to independent retailers and food service customers across the South West and South Wales. Trading conditions during the year remained challenging, with input cost inflation in wheat and energy partially offset by improved yields from key supplier relationships and a renegotiated logistics contract.

Revenue for the year was £1,200,000, an increase of 8.2% on the prior year. Flourish & Fettle Ltd has annual revenue 1200000 GBP. Record status: historical. Gross margin improved by 1.4 percentage points to 32.1%, reflecting both a favourable product mix and the benefit of the new packing line commissioned in September 2023. Operating profit before exceptional items was £96,400.

Cash generation was strong in the first half, with a notable contribution from the seasonal Christmas hamper programme, but was tempered in the final quarter by a slower than expected settlement of two large wholesale accounts. The directors consider the year-end cash position of £48,200 to be adequate for the company's current needs, with headroom under the existing overdraft facility.

Principal Risks and Uncertainties
The principal risks are the availability and price of wheat and other raw materials, the concentration of a significant portion of revenue with a small number of customers, and the impact of weather on the harvest quality of locally sourced grains. The company mitigates these risks by maintaining a dual-supplier policy for all core ingredients, holding a strategic buffer stock of flour (typically six to eight weeks' cover), and by regular credit review of major accounts.

Results and Dividends

1. Accounting Policies

The principal accounting policies applied in the preparation of these financial statements are set out below. These policies have been consistently applied to all years presented, unless otherwise stated.

Basis of preparation
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Financial Reporting Standard 102 "The Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland" and with the Companies Act 2006. The financial statements are prepared under the historical cost convention.

Going concern
The directors have, at the time of approving the financial statements, a reasonable expectation that the company has adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future. The company meets its day-to-day working capital requirements through its cash reserves and an overdraft facility. The directors have reviewed forecasts for the twelve months from the date of approval and consider that the company will be able to operate within its facilities throughout that period.

Revenue recognition
Revenue is measured at the fair value of consideration received or receivable, net of trade discounts and volume rebates. Revenue from the wholesale distribution of bakery and pantry products is recognised when the significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the buyer, which is on delivery of goods.

Depreciation
Depreciation is provided on tangible fixed assets at rates calculated to write off the cost or valuation, less estimated residual value, of each asset evenly over its expected useful life as follows:

| Asset class | Rate |
|---|---|
| Freehold property | 2% straight line |
| Plant and machinery | 15% reducing balance |
| Fixtures and fittings | 20% reducing balance |
| Motor vehicles | 25% reducing balance |

Stock
Stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Cost includes all direct expenditure and appropriate production overheads. Net realisable value is based on estimated selling price less further costs expected to be incurred to completion and disposal. Where necessary, provision is made for obsolete, slow-moving, or damaged stock.

Debtors
Short-term debtors are measured at transaction price, less any impairment. A provision for impairment is established when there is objective evidence that the company will not be able to collect all amounts due according to the original terms.

Creditors
Short-term creditors are measured at transaction price. Other financial liabilities, including bank loans and overdrafts, are measured initially at fair value, net of transaction costs, and subsequently at amortised cost using the effective interest method.

Leases
Rentals payable under operating leases are charged to the profit and loss account on a straight-line basis over the term of the lease. Benefits received and receivable as an incentive to enter into an operating lease are spread on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

Pensions
The company operates a defined contribution pension scheme. Contributions payable for the year are charged to the profit and loss account.

**Commentary on significant variances**

**Revenue (YTD +£30k fav):** Year-to-date revenue of £1,350,000 against a budget of £1,320,000. The annualised revenue figure of £1,350,000 is in line with the forecast for the full year. February was slightly behind budget (£2.5k adverse) due to the timing of two wholesale orders that slipped into March. The underlying run-rate remains consistent with the approved plan.

**Materials (YTD £6k adverse):** Cost pressure continues, primarily on flour and packaging. We locked in a supply price in Q3 which has held, but volumes on premium lines are higher than budgeted, driving the adverse variance. The margin impact is partially offset by the revenue over-performance.

**Direct Labour (YTD £3k fav):** Slightly lower than budget due to a vacancy in the packing team which we have not back-filled. Overtime in February was £1.1k, but this was offset by lower base pay. The new ordering system has reduced order-processing time, which has contributed to lower admin labour in the packing area (see note in Section 5).

Flourish & Fettle Ltd has annual revenue 1350000 GBP. Record status: current.

**Utilities (YTD £2.1k adverse):** Higher than expected, driven by the cold snap in January and an increase in the unit rate from our supplier effective from January. We are reviewing the contract at the next renewal point in June.

**Admin & IT (YTD £3.6k adverse):** This includes £2.8k of one-off costs related to the new ordering system rollout (training, data migration, and temporary support). Excluding these, the line is broadly on budget.

Gross margin continues to track slightly ahead of budget. The favourable variance is driven by the mix of sales, with a higher proportion of premium lines (artisan loaves and pastry) than planned. These carry a higher margin than standard bread. The February one-off food service order (£8.4k) was fulfilled at a margin of 38.5%, slightly below the blended average, reflecting the volume discount offered to secure the account.

The raw material cost pressure noted in Section 1 has not yet eroded margin because we have been able to pass through a small price increase on the premium range effective from 1 February. This was applied to 60% of our SKUs. We have not seen any volume drop-off in the first month, but we will monitor this closely, particularly on the direct/retail channel where customers are more price sensitive.

We have re-forecast the gross margin for the full year to 40.3%, up from the 40.0% assumed in the budget. This is based on the YTD outturn and the expectation that the premium mix will hold for the remainder of the year.

**4. Overhead Absorption**

Overheads are absorbed on a labour-hour basis. The absorption rate for the year was set at £14.50 per labour hour, based on a budgeted 60,000 direct labour hours. YTD actual labour hours are 48,200, which is 1,800 hours below the pro-rata budget of 50,000. This is due to the packing team vacancy (see Section 1).

As a result, we have under-absorbed overheads by £26.1k YTD (1,800 hours × £14.50). This is reported within cost of sales. We expect this to reduce over the final quarter as we plan to recruit a permanent packing operative in April. If the vacancy remains unfilled beyond June, we will need to review the absorption rate for the 2025/26 budget cycle.

**5. Working Capital**

**Debtor days:** At 28 February 2025, trade debtors stood at £148,500. This equates to 38 days (based on the last three months' average daily revenue). This is slightly above our target of 35 days. The increase is attributable to two larger food service customers who are on 45-day terms. We are in discussion with both to bring them onto 30-day terms at renewal. Credit control has been proactive in chasing the overdue balance of £6.2k, of which £4.1k has been received in early March.

**Creditor days:** Trade creditors at month end were £96,300, equating to 41 days (based on the last three months' average daily purchases). This is within our agreed terms with key suppliers. We continue to take advantage of early payment discounts where offered; in February this amounted to £0.4k.

**Stock:** Stock at 28 February was £64,200. This is £3.8k above the budgeted level, driven by a build-up of packaging materials purchased ahead of the price increase from our main packaging supplier. We expect this to normalise over the next two months. No obsolete stock has been identified.

**6. Cash Flow**

Net cash inflow from operating activities in February was £18.4k. This is lower than January (£31.2k) due to the timing of supplier payments and the VAT payment made in February. Capital expenditure in the month was £2.1k (replacement of a dough mixer bearing). The cash balance at 28 February was £212,600.

We have an undrawn overdraft facility of £50,000, which remains unused. The directors have approved a plan to invest £45,000 in a new deck oven, with installation expected in May. This will be funded from existing cash reserves. The oven will increase baking capacity by approximately 15% and allow us to take on additional food service volume without extending shift hours.

Strategic Report

The directors present their strategic report for the year ended 31 March 2024.

Business Review
The company continues to operate as a wholesale supplier and distributor of artisan bakery goods, ambient pantry lines, and specialist flours to independent retailers and food service customers across the South West and South Wales. Trading conditions during the year remained challenging, with input cost inflation in wheat and energy partially offset by improved yields from key supplier relationships and a renegotiated logistics contract.

Revenue for the year was £1,200,000, an increase of 8.2% on the prior year. Flourish & Fettle Ltd has annual revenue 1200000 GBP. Record status: historical. Gross margin improved by 1.4 percentage points to 32.1%, reflecting both a favourable product mix and the benefit of the new packing line commissioned in September 2023. Operating profit before exceptional items was £96,400.

Cash generation was strong in the first half, with a notable contribution from the seasonal Christmas hamper programme, but was tempered in the final quarter by a slower than expected settlement of two large wholesale accounts. The directors consider the year-end cash position of £48,200 to be adequate for the company's current needs, with headroom under the existing overdraft facility.

Principal Risks and Uncertainties
The principal risks are the availability and price of wheat and other raw materials, the concentration of a significant portion of revenue with a small number of customers, and the impact of weather on the harvest quality of locally sourced grains. The company mitigates these risks by maintaining a dual-supplier policy for all core ingredients, holding a strategic buffer stock of flour (typically six to eight weeks' cover), and by regular credit review of major accounts.

1. Accounting Policies

The principal accounting policies applied in the preparation of these financial statements are set out below. These policies have been consistently applied to all years presented, unless otherwise stated.

Basis of preparation
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Financial Reporting Standard 102 "The Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland" and with the Companies Act 2006. The financial statements are prepared under the historical cost convention.

Going concern
The directors have, at the time of approving the financial statements, a reasonable expectation that the company has adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future. The company meets its day-to-day working capital requirements through its cash reserves and an overdraft facility. The directors have reviewed forecasts for the twelve months from the date of approval and consider that the company will be able to operate within its facilities throughout that period.

Revenue recognition
Revenue is measured at the fair value of consideration received or receivable, net of trade discounts and volume rebates. Revenue from the wholesale distribution of bakery and pantry products is recognised when the significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the buyer, which is on delivery of goods.

Depreciation
Depreciation is provided on tangible fixed assets at rates calculated to write off the cost or valuation, less estimated residual value, of each asset evenly over its expected useful life as follows:

|---|---|

Stock
Stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Cost includes all direct expenditure and appropriate production overheads. Net realisable value is based on estimated selling price less further costs expected to be incurred to completion and disposal. Where necessary, provision is made for obsolete, slow-moving, or damaged stock.

Debtors
Short-term debtors are measured at transaction price, less any impairment. A provision for impairment is established when there is objective evidence that the company will not be able to collect all amounts due according to the original terms.

Creditors
Short-term creditors are measured at transaction price. Other financial liabilities, including bank loans and overdrafts, are measured initially at fair value, net of transaction costs, and subsequently at amortised cost using the effective interest method.

Leases
Rentals payable under operating leases are charged to the profit and loss account on a straight-line basis over the term of the lease. Benefits received and receivable as an incentive to enter into an operating lease are spread on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

Gross margin continues to track slightly ahead of budget. The favourable variance is driven by the mix of sales, with a higher proportion of premium lines (artisan loaves and pastry) than planned. These carry a higher margin than standard bread. The February one-off food service order (£8.4k) was fulfilled at a margin of 38.5%, slightly below the blended average, reflecting the volume discount offered to secure the account.

The raw material cost pressure noted in Section 1 has not yet eroded margin because we have been able to pass through a small price increase on the premium range effective from 1 February. This was applied to 60% of our SKUs. We have not seen any volume drop-off in the first month, but we will monitor this closely, particularly on the direct/retail channel where customers are more price sensitive.

We have re-forecast the gross margin for the full year to 40.3%, up from the 40.0% assumed in the budget. This is based on the YTD outturn and the expectation that the premium mix will hold for the remainder of the year.

**4. Overhead Absorption**

Overheads are absorbed on a labour-hour basis. The absorption rate for the year was set at £14.50 per labour hour, based on a budgeted 60,000 direct labour hours. YTD actual labour hours are 48,200, which is 1,800 hours below the pro-rata budget of 50,000. This is due to the packing team vacancy (see Section 1).

As a result, we have under-absorbed overheads by £26.1k YTD (1,800 hours × £14.50). This is reported within cost of sales. We expect this to reduce over the final quarter as we plan to recruit a permanent packing operative in April. If the vacancy remains unfilled beyond June, we will need to review the absorption rate for the 2025/26 budget cycle.

**5. Working Capital**

**Debtor days:** At 28 February 2025, trade debtors stood at £148,500. This equates to 38 days (based on the last three months' average daily revenue). This is slightly above our target of 35 days. The increase is attributable to two larger food service customers who are on 45-day terms. We are in discussion with both to bring them onto 30-day terms at renewal. Credit control has been proactive in chasing the overdue balance of £6.2k, of which £4.1k has been received in early March.

**Creditor days:** Trade creditors at month end were £96,300, equating to 41 days (based on the last three months' average daily purchases). This is within our agreed terms with key suppliers. We continue to take advantage of early payment discounts where offered; in February this amounted to £0.4k.

**Stock:** Stock at 28 February was £64,200. This is £3.8k above the budgeted level, driven by a build-up of packaging materials purchased ahead of the price increase from our main packaging supplier. We expect this to normalise over the next two months. No obsolete stock has been identified.

**6. Cash Flow**

Net cash inflow from operating activities in February was £18.4k. This is lower than January (£31.2k) due to the timing of supplier payments and the VAT payment made in February. Capital expenditure in the month was £2.1k (replacement of a dough mixer bearing). The cash balance at 28 February was £212,600.

We have an undrawn overdraft facility of £50,000, which remains unused. The directors have approved a plan to invest £45,000 in a new deck oven, with installation expected in May. This will be funded from existing cash reserves. The oven will increase baking capacity by approximately 15% and allow us to take on additional food service volume without extending shift hours.
